title: Cross-Validation: Penalty Tuning and Model Selection
text: Ridge penalties stabilise niche estimates sample sizes small environmental variables correlated. nicher supports three penalty knobs: Setting penalty high -regularises (biased niche); setting low -regularises (high variance). Cross-validation selects penalty strength maximises --sample log-likelihood.

code: library(nicher) set.seed(42)  fit_base <- optimize_niche(   env_occ    = example_env_occ_2d,   env_m      = example_env_m_2d,   likelihood = "weighted",   num_starts = 5L,   breadth    = 0.45,   prior_mu_lambda = 0,   verbose    = FALSE ) fit_base #> -- nicher optimization result -- #>   Likelihood : weighted  #>   Starts     : 6 (converged: 6 ) #>   Best loglik: -645.0662  #>   Convergence: 1  #>   eta        : 1  #>   Variables  : bio1WH, bio12WH

title: Cross-Validation: Penalty Tuning and Model Selection
text: cv_nicher() refits model train fold (warm-started full-data optimum) scores held-fold using un-penalised log-likelihood.
code: cv_base <- cv_nicher(   fit     = fit_base,   env_occ = example_env_occ_2d,   env_m   = example_env_m_2d,   type    = "kfold",   k       = 5L,   seed    = 42L,   verbose = FALSE ) cv_base #> -- nicher_cv result -- #>   Type     : kfold (k = 5)  #>   Family   : weighted  #>   Folds    : 5  #>   CV loglik: -650.923 (per-occ: -8.9168 )

title: Cross-Validation: Penalty Tuning and Model Selection
text: Fit models different penalty levels compare CV log-likelihoods. Higher (less negative) CV log-likelihood indicates better --sample fit. penalty value maximises cv_loglik best choice:
code: lambdas <- c(0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0) cv_results <- data.frame(   lambda   = lambdas,   cv_loglik     = NA_real_,   cv_loglik_mean = NA_real_ )  for (i in seq_along(lambdas)) {   fit_i <- optimize_niche(     env_occ    = example_env_occ_2d,     env_m      = example_env_m_2d,     likelihood = "weighted",     num_starts = 5L,     breadth    = 0.45,     prior_mu_lambda = lambdas[i],     verbose    = FALSE   )   cv_i <- cv_nicher(     fit     = fit_i,     env_occ = example_env_occ_2d,     env_m   = example_env_m_2d,     type    = "kfold",     k       = 5L,     seed    = 42L,     verbose = FALSE   )   cv_results$cv_loglik[i]      <- cv_i$cv_loglik   cv_results$cv_loglik_mean[i] <- cv_i$cv_loglik_mean }  cv_results #>   lambda cv_loglik cv_loglik_mean #> 1    0.0 -650.9230      -8.916754 #> 2    0.5 -656.6578      -8.995313 #> 3    1.0 -658.5260      -9.020904 #> 4    2.0 -660.9557      -9.054188 #> 5    5.0 -665.4376      -9.115583 best_idx <- which.max(cv_results$cv_loglik) cat("Best lambda:", cv_results$lambda[best_idx], "\n") #> Best lambda: 0 cat("CV loglik  :", cv_results$cv_loglik[best_idx], "\n") #> CV loglik  : -650.923

title: Cross-Validation: Penalty Tuning and Model Selection
text: CV can also compare different likelihood families. Refit family data compare --sample log-likelihoods:
code: families <- c("presence_only", "weighted", "ip_weighted") cv_family <- data.frame(   family         = families,   cv_loglik      = NA_real_,   cv_loglik_mean = NA_real_,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  for (i in seq_along(families)) {   fam <- families[i]   needs_m <- fam %in% c("weighted", "ip_weighted")   fit_i <- optimize_niche(     env_occ    = example_env_occ_2d,     env_m      = if (needs_m) example_env_m_2d else NULL,     likelihood = fam,     num_starts = 5L,     breadth    = 0.45,     verbose    = FALSE   )   cv_i <- cv_nicher(     fit     = fit_i,     env_occ = example_env_occ_2d,     env_m   = if (needs_m) example_env_m_2d else NULL,     type    = "kfold",     k       = 5L,     seed    = 42L,     verbose = FALSE   )   cv_family$cv_loglik[i]      <- cv_i$cv_loglik   cv_family$cv_loglik_mean[i] <- cv_i$cv_loglik_mean }  cv_family #>          family cv_loglik cv_loglik_mean #> 1 presence_only -630.3632      -8.635113 #> 2      weighted -658.5260      -9.020904 #> 3   ip_weighted -640.1458      -8.769120

title: Cross-Validation: Penalty Tuning and Model Selection
text: Spatial autocorrelation: Random k-fold CV assumes exchangeable observations. spatially autocorrelated data, CV log-likelihood may optimistic. Spatial-block CV planned future release. Computational cost: LOO large nn (e.g. 500+) runs one refit per observation. Consider type = "kfold", k = 10L faster proxy. Different normalisation: Presence-weighted families different likelihood normalising constants, CV log-likelihoods strictly comparable. Use comparison diagnostic rather formal test.

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
text: Constructs lower‑triangular Cholesky factor \(\mathbf{L}\) \(d \times d\) correlation matrix using C‑vine method described Lewandowski, Kurowicka & Joe (2009). factor satisfies \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top\) \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{R}) = 1\).

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
code: cvine_cholesky(v, d, eta = 1)

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
text: v Numeric vector unconstrained reals, one C‑vine edge. length must \(d(d-1)/2\). \(d = 2\), single value required. order follows **level‑major** sequence: first edges level 1 (.e., variable 1 later variable), edges level 2 (variable 2 later variables, conditioned variable 1), . d Integer, dimension target correlation matrix (\(d \ge 1\)). eta Positive numeric shape parameter LKJ‑C‑vine prior (default 1). \(\eta = 1\) gives uniform distribution correlation matrices; larger values concentrate mass near identity.

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
text: \(d \times d\) lower‑triangular matrix \(\mathbf{L}\)   positive diagonal entries \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top\)   valid correlation matrix (unit diagonal, positive definite). \(d = 1\),   returns \(1 \times 1\) matrix entry 1.

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
text: algorithm proceeds three steps: element v mapped unit interval via         logistic (sigmoid) function, transformed partial correlation         \((-1, 1)\) using quantile function symmetric Beta         distribution shape \(\phi_k = \eta + (d - k - 2)/2\)         (level \(k\), 0‑indexed). table partial correlations converted unconditional         correlations using Yule–Kendall recursion (vine recursion). new row \(j\) (starting \(j = 2\)), algorithm         solves triangular system obtain first \(j-1\) entries         row, sets diagonal entry maintain unit row norm. resulting \(\mathbf{L}\) can used directly construct correlation matrix (tcrossprod(L)), build covariance matrix scaling standard deviations.

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
text: Lewandowski, D., Kurowicka, D., & Joe, H. (2009). Generating random correlation matrices based vines extended onion method. *Journal Multivariate Analysis*, 100(9), 1989–2001. doi:10.1016/j.jmva.2009.04.008

title: Build Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix from C‑vine partial correlations — cvine_cholesky
code: # For a 2x2 correlation matrix, we need one parameter v <- 0.5 L <- cvine_cholesky(v, d = 2, eta = 1) R <- tcrossprod(L) print(R) #>           [,1]      [,2] #> [1,] 1.0000000 0.2449187 #> [2,] 0.2449187 1.0000000  # For 3 dimensions, we need 3 parameters (d*(d-1)/2 = 3) v <- c(0.1, -0.2, 0.8) L <- cvine_cholesky(v, d = 3) R <- tcrossprod(L) all.equal(diag(R), rep(1, 3)) # Should be TRUE #> [1] TRUE

"skew_normal": presence-fit multivariate         skew-normal niche         (Azzalini & Capitanio 1999, J. R. Stat. Soc. Ser. B 61(3):         579-602):         $$S(x) \propto \phi_p(x - \mu; \Sigma) \, \Phi\left(           \sum_k \alpha_k \, (x_k - \mu_k) / \sigma_k \right).$$         Adds length-p skewness vector \(\alpha\)         existing \((\mu, \Sigma)\) parameters. \(\alpha = 0\)         recovers symmetric Gaussian niche exactly.         Sobol-start machinery samples \(\alpha_k\)         \([-3, 3]\) (Azzalini & Capitanio 1999, Sec. 5). "skew_normal_weighted": paper Eq. 5 SN         density place Gaussian, plus ridge         prior \(\log \sigma\) used "weighted".         Defaults inherit "weighted". "skew_t": presence-fit multivariate         non-central skew-t (NCST) density (Branco & Dey 2001, J.         Multivariate Analysis 79(1):99-113):         $$T = \mu + X \sqrt{r/Y}, \quad X \sim SN_p(0, \Sigma, \alpha),                                                Y \sim \chi^2_r.$$         Adds single degrees--freedom parameter log_r         top skew-normal layout. Smaller \(r\) = heavier         tails; \(r \\infty\) recovers "skew_normal".         marginal density closed form, computed         32-node Gauss-Laguerre quadrature \(\chi^2_r\)         mixing variable. Sobol-start machinery samples log_r         \([\log 2, \log 100]\). "skew_t_weighted": paper Eq. 5 NCST         density place Gaussian, plus ridge prior         \(\log \sigma\) used "weighted". Defaults         inherit "weighted". multimodal long-tailed env_m, consider z-scoring env_occ env_m variables comparable spread (e.g. z-score quantile-rank); ridge prior uniform across axes.
